lessons.title: Common Diseases: Newcastle, Avian Influenza, and Marek's
lessons.body: Newcastle disease is the number one killer of village chickens in Africa. It spreads through droppings, nasal discharge, and contaminated feed, water, and equipment. Signs include gasping, coughing, twisting of the neck (torticollis), paralysis, and sudden death. There is no treatment. Vaccinate chicks at day 7 with NDV (Newcastle disease virus) vaccine via eye drop, then repeat at 4 weeks and every 3 months. In outbreak areas, use I-2 vaccine, which is heat-tolerant. Avian influenza (bird flu) is also deadly. It causes swollen heads, blue combs, and rapid death. Report any sudden deaths to a vet immediately. Do not eat or sell sick birds. Marek's disease causes paralysis of legs and wings, often in birds 8â24 weeks old. It spreads through feather dust. Vaccinate day-old chicks at the hatchery with Marek's vaccine (HVT or Rispens). There is no cure. For all three, prevention is key: buy chicks from certified hatcheries, keep different age groups separate, and disinfect shoes and equipment before entering the coop. In Africa, many smallholders lose 50â80% of flocks to Newcastle each year. Simple vaccination can save your flock. Always store vaccines in a cold chain (2â8Â°C) and use within 2 hours of mixing. If you see symptoms, isolate sick birds and call a vet or extension officer. Do not borrow or share equipment with neighbours during an outbreak. Burn or bury dead birds deeply (1 metre) away from water sources. Remember: healthy birds are productive birds.

lessons.title: Vaccination Schedules and Administration Techniques
lessons.body: A proper vaccination schedule protects your layers from costly diseases. For layers in Africa, follow this core schedule: Day 1: Marek's (at hatchery). Day 7: Newcastle (NDV) + Infectious Bronchitis (IB) â eye drop. Day 14: Gumboro (IBD) â drinking water. Day 21: Newcastle + IB â eye drop or drinking water. Day 28: Gumboro â drinking water. Week 6: Fowl Typhoid â injection. Week 8: Newcastle + IB + EDS â injection. Week 10: Fowl Cholera â injection. Week 16: Newcastle + IB + EDS â injection. Then every 3 months: Newcastle booster. For eye drop: hold chick, drop one drop into open eye, release. For drinking water: withdraw water for 2 hours, mix vaccine in clean water (no chlorine) with skim milk powder (2g per litre) to neutralise chlorine, then let birds drink within 1 hour. For injection: use subcutaneous route in the neck or intramuscular in breast muscle. Use a new needle every 50 birds. Always keep vaccines cold: use a cooler with ice packs. Never freeze Newcastle or Gumboro vaccines. Reconstitute only one vial at a time and use within 2 hours. Record every vaccination: date, vaccine name, batch number, and number of birds. This helps you track coverage and troubleshoot. If you miss a booster, revaccinate as soon as possible. In hot climates, work early morning or evening to reduce stress. Handle birds gently. After vaccination, give vitamins and electrolytes in water for 2 days to reduce stress. A well-vaccinated flock can reduce mortality from 40% to under 5%.

lessons.title: Parasite Control: Internal and External
lessons.body: Parasites steal nutrients and cause anaemia, weight loss, and reduced egg production. Internal parasites include roundworms, tapeworms, and coccidia. Signs: pale comb, diarrhoea, worms in droppings, and poor growth. Deworm every 3 months with Levamisole (10mg/kg body weight) or Piperazine (100mg/kg) in drinking water. For coccidiosis (bloody droppings), use Amprolium (1g per 2 litres of water for 5 days) or Sulphaquinoxaline. Always follow withdrawal periods: 7 days for meat, 0 days for eggs (check label). External parasites: mites, lice, fleas, and ticks. They cause itching, feather loss, and skin wounds. Treat the coop and birds. For mites: spray coop with permethrin (1:100 dilution) or use diatomaceous earth in dust baths. For lice: dust birds with carbaryl powder (5%) under wings and around vent. Repeat after 10 days to kill newly hatched eggs. For ticks: use amitraz spray (1:200) on birds and environment. Keep litter dry: parasites thrive in damp conditions. Replace wet litter immediately. Provide dust baths: mix wood ash, sand, and diatomaceous earth in a shallow box. This natural method reduces external parasites. Rotate poultry runs if possible. In Africa, many smallholders use wood ash and tobacco leaves as traditional remedies, but these are less effective than modern treatments. Always consult a vet before using any drug. Never use human dewormers on chickens without veterinary advice. Record treatment dates and drugs used. After treatment, give vitamins to boost immunity. A parasite-free flock lays 20% more eggs.

lessons.title: Recognizing Signs of Illness and Taking Action
lessons.body: Early recognition saves flocks. Learn to spot sick birds quickly. Healthy layers are active, alert, with bright red combs and clean vents. Sick birds show: drooping wings, ruffled feathers, closed eyes, pale or blue combs, loss of appetite, reduced egg production, watery or bloody diarrhoea, coughing, sneezing, and sitting in corners. Check your flock at least twice daily: morning and evening. Look for birds that are separate from the group. Pick them up: feel the crop (should be full at night, empty in morning), check the vent for pasty droppings, and look for external parasites. If you see one sick bird, isolate it immediately in a separate cage with its own feed and water. Wear gloves and wash hands after handling. Record symptoms: what you see, when it started, how many birds affected. Take a photo or video if possible. Call a vet or extension officer within 24 hours. Do not wait. For common issues: if birds gasp and twist necks, suspect Newcastle â isolate and report. If bloody droppings, suspect coccidiosis â start Amprolium. If swollen head and blue comb, suspect Avian Influenza â report immediately to authorities. Do not sell or eat sick birds. Do not move birds to other farms. If a bird dies, wrap it in plastic and bury deep (1 metre) or burn. Disinfect the area. After an outbreak, clean and disinfect the entire coop with 2% caustic soda or 1% formalin. Rest the coop for 2 weeks before restocking. Keep records: date, symptoms, action taken, outcome. This helps you learn and prevent future problems. Quick action can save 80% of your flock.

lessons.title: Biosecurity Measures to Prevent Disease Outbreaks
lessons.body: Biosecurity means keeping diseases out. It is the cheapest and most effective health tool. Start with a footbath at the entrance of your coop. Use a plastic basin with 2% caustic soda or 1% formalin. Refresh daily. Keep a separate pair of boots and overalls for the coop. Never wear them outside. Limit visitors. If they must enter, they must wear clean boots and overalls. Do not let them bring birds or eggs from other farms. Quarantine new birds for 30 days before adding to your flock. Keep different age groups in separate houses. All-in, all-out is best: raise one batch, sell or cull, then clean and rest before the next batch. Clean and disinfect feeders and drinkers weekly. Use 1% chlorine solution or commercial disinfectant. Let them dry in sun. Keep feed in sealed containers, off the floor, to prevent rodents. Control rats and wild birds: they carry diseases. Use traps and screens. Keep litter dry: replace wet spots daily. Provide good ventilation to reduce ammonia. Avoid stress: overcrowding, heat, and poor feed lower immunity. Vaccinate on schedule. Keep a record of all visitors and any disease events. If you see a dead bird, remove it immediately. Do not compost dead birds near the coop. In Africa, many outbreaks start from sharing equipment or buying live birds at markets. Buy chicks from certified hatcheries. Do not mix your birds with neighbours' flocks. If there is an outbreak nearby, stop all visitors and do not sell birds. A strong biosecurity plan can reduce disease risk by 90%. It costs little but saves a lot.

lessons.title: Working with Veterinarians and Diagnostic Labs
lessons.body: A good veterinarian is your best partner. Find one before you have a problem. Ask your local extension officer or fellow farmers for recommendations. In many African countries, the government provides free or subsidised vet services through the Department of Veterinary Services. Keep the vet's phone number saved. When you call, be ready to describe: number of birds, age, symptoms, when they started, and any recent changes (feed, weather, new birds). If the vet cannot come, they may ask you to bring a live sick bird or a dead bird for post-mortem. For lab diagnosis, collect samples properly. For blood: use a sterile syringe, take 1â2 ml from the wing vein, put in a plain tube (red top). For swabs: use sterile swabs from trachea or cloaca, place in transport medium. For tissue: collect fresh liver, spleen, or lung from a recently dead bird (within 2 hours), put in a clean plastic bag on ice. Label clearly: your name, farm, date, bird age, and symptoms. Send to a diagnostic lab. In Africa, labs include: National Veterinary Research Institute (Nigeria), Central Veterinary Laboratory (Kenya), and Onderstepoort (South Africa). Many countries have regional labs. Ask your vet for the nearest. Results may take 3â7 days. While waiting, isolate sick birds and disinfect. When results come, follow the vet's treatment plan exactly. Do not guess. If you cannot afford a vet, use your extension officer or farmer groups. Some NGOs offer free diagnostic services. Keep records of all lab reports. This helps you track disease patterns. A vet can also help you design a vaccination schedule and biosecurity plan. Build a relationship: invite them for a farm visit once a year. Prevention is cheaper than treatment.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Health Management and Disease Prevention in African Layer Farming

In African layer farming, disease outbreaks can wipe out an entire flock's productivity within daysâturning a profitable egg business into a financial loss. Newcastle disease alone can cause up to 100% mortality in unvaccinated flocks, while Avian Influenza outbreaks trigger trade bans and culling that destroy livelihoods. This practical reference gives you the tools to protect your investment: actionable vaccination schedules, parasite control protocols, early illness detection, biosecurity measures, and guidance on working with veterinary professionals. Every recommendation here is designed for real African conditionsâlimited cold chain access, mixed-age flocks, free-range systems, and resource constraints.

1. Common Diseases: Newcastle, Avian Influenza, and Marek's

Newcastle Disease (ND) is the single most devastating disease for African layer farmers. It is caused by a paramyxovirus and spreads through contaminated feed, water, equipment, and wild birds. Symptoms include gasping, coughing, twisted necks (torticollis), greenish watery diarrhoea, and a sudden drop in egg production with soft-shelled or misshapen eggs. Mortality can reach 100% in unvaccinated flocks. In many African countries, ND is endemic and vaccination is mandatory for commercial operations.

Avian Influenza (AI) â particularly Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1 and H5N8 â poses a dual threat: bird mortality and human health risk. African outbreaks have been reported in Egypt, Nigeria, South Africa, and Burkina Faso. Symptoms include sudden death, swollen heads, purple discolouration of wattles and combs, and respiratory distress. There is no treatment; control relies on culling, quarantine, and compensation schemes. Reporting suspected AI to veterinary authorities is legally required in most African countries.

Marek's Disease (MD) is a herpesvirus that causes tumours in nerves and organs, leading to paralysis, weight loss, and death, typically in birds aged 8â24 weeks. It spreads through dander (feather dust) in the air and is extremely persistent in poultry houses. Vaccination at day-old is the only reliable prevention; there is no treatment. In Africa, where day-old chicks may be sourced from hatcheries with inconsistent vaccination records, always verify MD vaccination status before purchase.

2. Vaccination Schedules and Administration Techniques

Vaccination is the cornerstone of disease prevention, but in Africa, cold chain challenges mean you must plan carefully. Vaccines must be stored between 2â8Â°C; never freeze Newcastle or AI vaccines. Use a cooler box with ice packs when transporting. Administer vaccines in the early morning or late evening to reduce heat stress.

Table 1: Recommended Vaccination Schedule for Layer Chickens in Africa
Age Vaccine Route Notes
Day 1Marek's DiseaseSubcutaneous (neck)Given at hatchery; verify certificate
Day 7Newcastle (NDV) + IBEye drop / nasalUse reconstituted vaccine within 2 hours
Day 14Gumboro (IBD)Drinking waterWithhold water 1â2 hrs before
Day 21Newcastle (NDV) boosterDrinking waterAdd skim milk powder to water
Day 28Gumboro boosterDrinking waterCheck water quality; avoid chlorine
Week 6Newcastle (NDV)Intramuscular / wing webUse killed vaccine for long immunity
Week 8Fowl TyphoidIntramuscularWhere endemic (e.g., Nigeria, Kenya)
Week 10Newcastle + IBDrinking waterBooster before point of lay
Week 16Newcastle (killed)IntramuscularFinal booster before laying
Every 8â10 weeksNewcastle (live)Drinking waterContinue during laying for sustained immunity

Source: Adapted from FAO (2004). Recommendations for the Prevention, Control and Eradication of Newcastle Disease in Africa. FAO Animal Production and Health Paper 161. Rome: FAO. Available at: https://www.fao.org/3/y5162e/y5162e00.htm

3. Parasite Control: Internal and External

Parasites drain productivity silently. Internal parasites (roundworms, tapeworms, coccidia) cause weight loss, pale combs, and reduced egg production. External parasites (mites, lice, ticks, fleas) cause irritation, feather loss, and anaemia. In free-range and semi-intensive African systems, parasite pressure is higher due to contact with soil and wild birds.

Table 2: Common Parasites and Control Measures for African Layer Farms
Parasite Type Signs Treatment Prevention
Ascaridia (roundworm)InternalWeight loss, pale comb, diarrhoeaPiperazine or Levamisole in waterRegular deworming every 6â8 weeks; clean litter
Raillietina (tapeworm)InternalEmaciation, reduced layingPraziquantel or NiclosamideControl intermediate hosts (ants, beetles)
Eimeria (coccidia)InternalBloody droppings, huddlingAmprolium or SulphonamidesCoccidiostat in feed; dry litter management
Dermanyssus (red mite)ExternalAnaemia, restlessness, bite marksIvermectin or Permethrin sprayDust baths; treat perches and cracks
Menacanthus (lice)ExternalFeather damage, itchingInsecticidal dust or sprayRegular inspection; quarantine new birds
Argas (fowl tick)ExternalWeight loss, paralysis, anaemiaAcaricide spray on housingSeal cracks; rotate pastures

Source: Adapted from Permin, A. & Hansen, J.W. (1998). Epidemiology, Diagnosis and Control of Poultry Parasites. FAO Animal Health Manual No. 4. Rome: FAO. Available at: https://www.fao.org/3/x4571e/x4571e00.htm

4. Recognizing Signs of Illness and Taking Action

Early detection saves flocks. Train yourself and your workers to observe birds daily. Key warning signs include:

  • Respiratory: Sneezing, coughing, gasping, swollen sinuses, nasal discharge.
  • Digestive: Watery or bloody diarrhoea, reduced feed intake, crop stasis.
  • Behavioural: Huddling, isolation, reluctance to move, dropped wings.
  • Production: Sudden drop in egg production, soft-shelled or misshapen eggs.
  • Physical: Pale or purple comb/wattles, swollen joints, eye discharge, paralysis.

Action protocol: Isolate sick birds immediately. Record symptoms, number affected, and mortality. Contact your veterinarian within 24 hours. Do not sell or consume eggs or meat from sick birds. If Newcastle or AI is suspected, report to local veterinary authorities immediatelyâdo not wait.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Avian Influenza (AI) is a Zoonotic Disease

Avian Influenza can infect humans, causing severe illness and death. If you suspect AI (sudden deaths, swollen heads, purple combs), do not handle sick or dead birds without PPE (gloves, mask, goggles, boots). Do not eat or sell eggs/meat from affected flocks. Report immediately to veterinary authorities. In Africa, AI outbreaks have been confirmed in Egypt, Nigeria, South Africa, Burkina Faso, and Cameroon. Always follow national reporting protocols.

5. Biosecurity Measures to Prevent Disease Outbreaks

Biosecurity is your first line of defence and costs far less than treating a disease outbreak. Implement these measures consistently:

  • Footbaths: Place at every entry point. Use fresh disinfectant (e.g., 2% sodium hypochlorite or quaternary ammonium) and change daily.
  • Visitor control: Limit visitors. Require clean boots and overalls. Keep a visitor log.
  • All-in/all-out: Where possible, raise birds of the same age together. Clean and disinfect between batches.
  • Rodent and wild bird control: Use mesh screens, traps, and keep feed stored in sealed containers.
  • Water quality: Chlorinate drinking water (1â2 ppm free chlorine) and test regularly.
  • Dead bird disposal: Burn or deep-bury carcasses immediately. Never feed dead birds to other animals.
  • Equipment hygiene: Clean and disinfect feeders, drinkers, and egg trays weekly.
  • Quarantine new birds: Isolate for 2â3 weeks before introducing to the main flock.

6. Working with Veterinarians and Diagnostic Labs

A good relationship with a veterinarian is an investment, not a cost. In many African countries, government veterinary services offer free or subsidised diagnostic support. Private vets may charge consultation fees, but early diagnosis prevents catastrophic losses. When submitting samples to a diagnostic lab:

  • Collect samples from freshly dead or acutely sick birds (not decomposed ones).
  • Use sterile swabs for respiratory or cloacal samples; place in viral transport medium.
  • Label samples clearly with farm name, date, age of flock, and symptoms.
  • Keep samples cool (4Â°C) but do not freeze if submitting for bacterial culture.
  • Ask for a written report and follow-up advice on treatment and prevention.

In Africa, regional laboratories include: Nigerian Veterinary Research Institute (Vom), Kenya Veterinary Vaccines Production Institute (KEVEVAPI), Onderstepoort Veterinary Institute (South Africa), and National Veterinary Laboratory (Egypt). Contact your national veterinary authority for the nearest lab.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Vaccinate day-old chicks against Marek's at the hatchery; verify certificate.
  2. â Follow the Newcastle and Gumboro vaccination schedule without skipping boosters.
  3. â Deworm every 6â8 weeks; treat for external parasites monthly.
  4. â Observe flock daily for respiratory, digestive, and behavioural signs of illness.
  5. â Isolate sick birds immediately and contact your vet within 24 hours.
  6. â Maintain footbaths, visitor logs, and all-in/all-out batch management.
  7. â Store vaccines at 2â8Â°C; never freeze; use cooler boxes during transport.
  8. â Report suspected Newcastle or Avian Influenza to authorities immediately.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2019). Good Emergency Management Practice: The Essentials â A Guide to Preparing for Animal Health Emergencies. FAO Animal Production and Health Manual No. 24.
  • FAO (2004). Recommendations for the Prevention, Control and Eradication of Newcastle Disease in Africa. FAO Animal Production and Health Paper 161.
  • Permin, A. & Hansen, J.W. (1998). Epidemiology, Diagnosis and Control of Poultry Parasites. FAO Animal Health Manual No. 4.
  • WOAH (World Organisation for Animal Health). Avian Influenza â Official Disease Information and Reporting Guidelines.
  • IFPRI (International Food Policy Research Institute). Poultry Sector in Africa â Research and Policy Briefs.

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme. For practical demonstrations, contact your local agricultural extension officer or veterinary services. Always adapt recommendations to your local regulations and disease prevalence.

quiz.q: Which disease causes twisting of the neck and has no treatment?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle disease causes torticollis and is viral with no cure.

quiz.q: At what age should chicks receive Marek's vaccine?
quiz.explanation: Marek's vaccine is given at day-old, usually at the hatchery.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given via eye drop at day 7?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle and Infectious Bronchitis are given by eye drop at day 7.

quiz.q: What is the correct storage temperature for most poultry vaccines?
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be kept in a cold chain at 2â8Â°C, not frozen.

quiz.q: How long after mixing a vaccine should it be used?
quiz.explanation: Reconstituted vaccines lose potency quickly and must be used within 2 hours.

quiz.q: Which internal parasite causes bloody droppings?
quiz.explanation: Coccidiosis causes bloody diarrhoea and is treated with Amprolium.

quiz.q: What is the withdrawal period for eggs after using most dewormers?
quiz.explanation: Most dewormers have zero egg withdrawal, but always check the label.

quiz.q: Which external parasite treatment involves dusting birds with carbaryl powder?
quiz.explanation: Carbaryl powder is used for lice, applied under wings and around vent.

quiz.q: What is a natural method to reduce external parasites?
options: A) Dust bath with wood ash
quiz.explanation: Wood ash, sand, and diatomaceous earth in a dust bath help control parasites.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm layers?
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming every 3 months prevents internal parasite build-up.

quiz.q: Which sign indicates a sick bird?
quiz.explanation: Drooping wings, ruffled feathers, and closed eyes are signs of illness.

quiz.q: What should you do first when you see a sick bird?
quiz.explanation: Isolate sick birds immediately to prevent spread to healthy flock.

quiz.q: If birds show gasping and twisted necks, what disease should you suspect?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle disease causes respiratory distress and nervous signs.

quiz.q: How deep should you bury a dead bird?
quiz.explanation: Deep burial at 1 metre prevents scavengers and disease spread.

quiz.q: What is the best disinfectant for a footbath?
quiz.explanation: 2% caustic soda or 1% formalin is effective for footbaths.

quiz.q: How long should new birds be quarantined?
quiz.explanation: 30-day quarantine allows time for any latent diseases to appear.

quiz.q: Which biosecurity measure prevents disease introduction?
quiz.explanation: All-in, all-out reduces disease carryover between batches.

quiz.q: What should you do with feed to prevent rodents?
quiz.explanation: Sealed containers off the floor prevent rodent access.

quiz.q: Why is dry litter important?
quiz.explanation: Damp litter promotes parasites and bacteria; keep it dry.

quiz.q: What is the first step when calling a vet?
quiz.explanation: Describe number of birds, age, symptoms, and duration clearly.

quiz.q: Which sample is best for disease diagnosis from a dead bird?
quiz.explanation: Fresh liver, spleen, or lung tissue within 2 hours is ideal for lab tests.

quiz.q: How should blood samples be stored before sending to lab?
quiz.explanation: Blood samples should be kept cool on ice, not frozen.

quiz.q: What is the role of a veterinarian in layer farming?
options: B) Design vaccination and biosecurity plans
quiz.explanation: Vets help with prevention, diagnosis, and treatment plans.

quiz.q: Which disease requires immediate reporting to authorities?
quiz.explanation: Avian Influenza is a notifiable disease and must be reported.

quiz.q: What is the correct dilution for permethrin spray for mites?
quiz.explanation: Permethrin is diluted 1:100 for mite control in coops.

quiz.q: How often should you clean and disinfect drinkers?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning with 1% chlorine prevents biofilm and disease.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of a dust bath for birds?
quiz.explanation: Dust baths with ash or diatomaceous earth reduce mites and lice.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is given by injection at week 6?
quiz.explanation: Fowl Typhoid vaccine is given by injection around week 6.

quiz.q: What should you do if you miss a booster vaccination?
options: B) Revaccinate as soon as possible
quiz.explanation: Revaccinate immediately to restore immunity.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biosecurity risk?
quiz.explanation: Dirty boots can carry pathogens into the coop.
